title: Australia Is Nearly the Size of the US. Why Do 85% Hug the Coast?

minor: The 85 percent within 50 km figure comes from the 2001 Census (ABS Year Book 2004). The title and opening state it in the present tense, so a short 'by the 2001 census' or 'about' would be safer.
'Over a third of world iron ore comes from the Pilbara' is a slight rounding down. The source gives 38 percent for all of Australia, almost all of it from the Pilbara.
Canberra: 1908 is the Seat of Government Act (Yass-Canberra district). The Canberra site itself was fixed a year later, so 'the site chosen in 1908' is slightly loose.
'The range wrings much of the rain from Pacific air' and 'stone ruins still stand' (abandoned farms north of Goyder's Line) are true in general but have no listed source.
'Later lines crossed the whole interior' comes after the 1880s farm collapse, but the Overland Telegraph (1872) predates it. Read as 'later than Goyder in 1865' it works, but the order could confuse.
Kosciuszko is the highest point on the Australian mainland and in the Great Dividing Range. 'Its highest point' is correct, but it is not the highest in Australia (Heard Island is higher).
The First Fleet reached Botany Bay on 18-20 January and moved to Sydney Cove on 26 January. The script's 'anchored at Sydney Cove on 26 January' is fine, but the Botany Bay stop is skipped.

shots.vo: So why do most Australians live on the coast, leaving the middle empty?
The answer starts in 1788, on a small cove on the Pacific coast.
shots.prompt: Wooden sailing ships at anchor in a quiet wooded harbour cove at dawn, seen from a low headland; duotone archival plate, dark slate and one muted orange, no faces, no text, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: Draw a band 50 kilometres in from the shoreline, and it holds most of Australia's roughly 27 million people.

map.label: 50 km from the sea: 85% of people

shots.vo: Two in three Australians live in the eight capital cities, and seven of those eight sit beside the sea.
Sydney counted about 5.45 million people in 2023, and Melbourne about 5.21 million, together 40 percent of Australia.
Sydney and Perth face each other across about 3,300 kilometres, most of it dry country with few towns.
Perth, home to about 2.3 million people, is roughly 2,100 kilometres from Adelaide, the next capital to the east.
Darwin, the northern capital with about 150,000 people, sits closer to Jakarta than it does to Sydney.
Behind the east coast runs the Great Dividing Range, more than 3,500 kilometres of hills and plateaus.
Its highest point, Mount Kosciuszko, is only 2,228 metres, yet the range wrings much of the rain from Pacific air.
About half of Australia gets less than 300 millimetres of rain a year, a quarter of Sydney's average.

map.label: Under 300 mm of rain a year

shots.vo: Sydney's long-term average is about 1,213 millimetres a year, while Alice Springs, in the centre, gets about 283.
Alice Springs, the main town of the centre, is roughly 1,500 kilometres by road from both Adelaide and Darwin.
Geoscience Australia counts about 35 percent of the continent as getting so little rain that it is effectively desert.
Inland rivers drain toward Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre, about 15 metres below sea level, with no outlet to the sea.
Beneath the dry inland lies the Great Artesian Basin, spreading under about 22 percent of Australia.
The great exception is the Murray–Darling Basin, about a million square kilometres of the southeast fed by rivers.
It produces over a third of Australia's food, and about 2.3 million people live inside it.

US Geological Survey figures put Australia's 2023 output at about 960 million tonnes, the largest of any country.

At the 2021 census, only about 2 in every 100 Australians lived in areas classed as remote or very remote.

shots.vo: That leaves an average of about 3.5 people per square kilometre, against roughly 36 in the United States.
Was the centre always this empty, or did someone draw the lines that hold Australians at the rim?

shots.vo: Aboriginal people have lived on this continent for at least 65,000 years, by the dating of Madjedbebe rock shelter.
That date comes from a 2017 study in Nature; other researchers argue the evidence points closer to 50,000 years.

shots.vo: Their nations covered the whole continent, desert included, speaking more than 250 languages before 1788.
How many people lived here in 1788 is still debated, and the published estimates sit very far apart.
The ABS Year Book records estimates ranging from about 315,000 people to more than one million.
On 26 January 1788, eleven ships with about 1,400 to 1,500 people anchored at Sydney Cove, and the first European settlement is pinned on the coast.
About 50 kilometres west, the sandstone cliffs of the Blue Mountains held the new colony to the coastal plain.
For 25 years, settlers farmed the narrow strip between the ocean and those cliffs.

shots.vo: On the colony's maps, everything west of those cliffs stayed blank, unmapped by Europeans.

shots.vo: In May 1813, Gregory Blaxland, William Lawson and William Wentworth found a way across by following the ridges.
A road followed in 1815 to the new inland town of Bathurst, roughly 150 to 160 kilometres west of Sydney.
In 1844 Charles Sturt set out north from Adelaide hoping to find an inland sea.
And his route stops at a stony desert, which is marked on the map where the settled edge ends.

map.label: Stony desert: the settled edge ends

shots.vo: In 1865, after a severe drought, South Australia's surveyor-general George Goyder rode north to map where it had struck.
He drew a line across the map, marking where rainfall seemed reliable enough to farm, and where it was not.
In the wetter 1870s, the government opened land beyond Goyder's Line to wheat farming.
Wheat farmers followed with horse-drawn ploughs, pushing north into country Goyder had marked as unreliable.

shots.vo: When drier years returned in the 1880s, many of those farms were abandoned, and their stone ruins still stand.

shots.vo: Goyder's Line still roughly marks where cropping gives way to grazing in South Australia today.
Later lines crossed the whole interior, but they carried messages, freight and passengers rather than new settlers.
In 1872 the Overland Telegraph Line ran about 3,200 kilometres from Adelaide to Darwin, through Alice Springs.
In 1917 the Trans-Australian Railway crossed the Nullarbor Plain, including one dead-straight stretch of 478 kilometres.
The railway from Adelaide only reached Darwin in 2004, linking the south and north coasts by rail for the first time.
Back on 1 January 1901, six colonies federated into one country under a new Constitution.

Section 125 places the seat of government in New South Wales, at least 100 miles, about 160 kilometres, from Sydney.

shots.vo: In 1973 the federal government chose Albury–Wodonga, on the Murray River, as a planned national growth centre.
The plan aimed for about 300,000 residents by 2000; the 2021 census counted fewer than 100,000.
So today the argument splits the same map two ways: spread Australians out, or let the coastal cities keep growing.

map.label: Spread out, or grow the rim?

shots.vo: Its supporters point to coastal house prices, long commutes, and country towns that need workers for schools and hospitals.
Would you move 300 kilometres inland for a cheaper house, if your job could come with you?
In 2020–21, Australia's capital cities lost a net 43,000 people to the regions through moves within the country.
The ABS called it a record, and supporters of regional growth read it as proof that people will move.
The other side's case, in its strongest form, starts with where the country's money is actually made.
A 2014 Grattan Institute study found that just 0.2 percent of Australia's land produces about 80 percent of its economic activity.

stat.label: of economic activity on 0.2% of the land (Grattan Institute, 2014)

shots.vo: Its authors argued that dense cities let firms and workers find each other, something small towns struggle to match.
Others add the water limit: beyond the wet rim and the Murray–Darling, rainfall is low and unreliable for big cities.
Even coastal Perth now draws close to half its drinking water from the ocean, through two desalination plants.
Australia has moved water on a very large scale before, for example through the Snowy Mountains Scheme, built between 1949 and 1974.
More than 100,000 people from over 30 countries built its dams, tunnels and power stations.

shots.vo: Which case wins depends partly on what happens next, and three possible changes can already be drawn on the map.
The first is the north, which a 2015 federal White Paper put at about 40 percent of Australia's land.

map.label: The north: about 40% of the land

shots.vo: The same paper counted about 1.3 million people there, or roughly five percent of the national population.

shots.vo: The north is not dry: Darwin averages about 1,700 millimetres of rain, nearly all of it in the wet season.
The Ord River scheme dammed Lake Argyle in 1971 to store that seasonal water for farms around Kununurra.
In 2016 Canberra set up the Northern Australia Infrastructure Facility with $5 billion, raised to $7 billion in 2021.
shots.prompt: A new sealed road running straight through red tropical scrub toward low hills, a road crew's machinery parked at the edge; top third plain dark slate sky; duotone archival plate, dark slate and muted orange

shots.vo: If such projects work, towns could grow along the tropical rivers; if they stall, the north stays thinly settled.
The second change comes from the sea itself, pressing on the rim where most Australians already live.
A 2009 federal report put between 157,000 and 247,600 existing homes at risk under a 1.1-metre sea-level rise.

stat.label: at risk under a 1.1 m sea-level rise (Dept of Climate Change, 2009)

shots.prompt: Low beachfront houses behind a narrow dune with a high tide washing close, grey sky; top third plain dark slate sky; duotone archival plate, dark slate and muted orange

shots.vo: It used 1.1 metres as a high-end scenario for 2100; how fast the sea will actually rise remains a projection.
If the water does rise, the shoreline could shift inland in low-lying suburbs, while the cities stay by the sea.
The third change is quieter: whether the 2020–21 drift to the regions turns out to be a trend or a blip.
If it lasts, the coastal band may thicken into a second ring of regional towns, rather than reach the centre.
Notice that none of the three scenarios points people at the dry centre itself, and the rain map offers one reason why.
Australia's population map closely follows its rainfall map, with history and economics adding to the pattern.
Next, a country whose people crowd not along a coast but along a border: Canada, beside the United States.
